frames.narration: A customer pays 100.00 by card, and the platform keeps a 3.00 fee. The accounts are cash at the bank, customer wallets, merchant payable and fee revenue, and every balance will be derived from the journal.
The service builds one entry: debit cash at the bank 10000, credit merchant payable 9700, credit fee revenue 300. Debits 10000, credits 10000, so it balances and is appended.
A buggy job tries to post a debit of 5000 and a credit of 4900. The journal refuses it and names the difference of 100. Without that check, 100 cents would exist in the books with no source.

Two payments arrive in the same instant. The journal appends two entries, #2 and #3, and merchant payable is the sum. A balance column that reads, adds and writes back would let the second write overwrite the first.
The customer returns the first purchase. The refund is a new entry in the opposite direction: debit merchant payable 9700, debit fee revenue 300, credit cash 10000. The payment is not touched.
Someone tops up a wallet by mistake. Nobody edits the entry. A reversal swaps its debits and credits as entry #6, and both stay in the journal for the audit trail.

At night the auditor adds all debits and all credits. They are equal, so the difference is 0. That proves nothing was added or lost on the way, though not that the amounts are right: the bank statement checks that.
